To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the quantitative mRNA-protein correlations among the 275 protein-coding genes of the human chromosome 18 are low in the liver, and even lower in HepG2 cells, which can be explained by the fact that the existing proteomic methods are not sensitive enough to detect all the proteins encoded by these genes.
the mRNA-protein correlation for chromosome 18 is 0.15 in human liver and 0.22 in HepG2 cells, and the median mRNA-protein ratio is 0.5 in human liver and in HepG2 cell.
the correlations between mRNA and protein levels for the 275 predicted protein-coding genes on human Chromosome 18 are low, but the reasons for these low correlations are different among the genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic analysis of quantitative mRNA-proteomics data obtained by the application of different analytical methods for the same set of biological samples.
the following questions: 1) Why are the correlations between mRNA and protein levels so low among the 275 predicted protein-coding genes on human chromosome 18?

the following questions: (1) How many proteins encoded by the genes of chromosome 18 are missing from the proteome of liver and HepG 2 cells?; (2) Why are the correlations between mRNA and protein levels for the selected 275 genes on human chromosome 18 so low?; (3) Can the existing analytical proteomic approaches be applied to detect missing proteins?; (4) Can the missing proteins be detected using a combination of different proteomic approaches?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the low mRNA-protein correlations among the 275 chromosome 18 genes are due to the fact that the majority of these proteins are not expressed at all in liver and/or HepG2 cells, and that the existing proteomics methods are not sufficiently sensitive to detect them.
there are no significant correlations between transcriptomic and proteomic data for the 275 chromosome 18 encoded genes in HepG2 cells or human liver.

the low correlation of mRNA and protein levels in the human liver and in HepG2 cells is a result of methodological limitations and that the missing proteins are not expressed or are expressed at a very low level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no evidence of a global under- or overestimation of mRNA-protein ratios by proteomics methods.

, although we were not able to detect all proteins encoded by the selected 275 genes, our results indicate that most of them are expressed in human liver and that the majority of them are present in human HepG2 cells as well.

we have shown that it is possible to estimate quantitative mRNA-protein correlations for a large set of human chromosome 18 genes using targeted and non-targeted MS-based proteomic methods and RNA-Seq transcriptomic methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the existing proteomic technologies are not yet capable of providing reliable quantitative information about low-abundant proteins.

the existing analytical methods are not sufficiently accurate for the detection of low-abundance proteins, and therefore, the low correlations between mRNA and protein levels for the majority of chromosome 18 genes can be explained by the lack of detection of the majority of these proteins.
, while the existing analytical methods are able to detect the presence of proteins in the cells, their sensitivity is not high enough to detect proteins that are expressed at low levels.
